name: Maghrebi Andalusi nuba
lineage: Maghrebi Andalusi nuba (al-Āla in Moroccan usage, gharnati in Algerian, ma'luf in Tunisian and Libyan) classical modal-suite tradition descended directly from the medieval Andalusi music of al-Andalus (Muslim Spain, ninth-fifteenth centuries) through the post-1492 expulsion-diaspora that brought the Andalusi musical tradition to the North African Maghreb. Each of the four primary Maghrebi traditions preserves a regional-variant repertoire: Moroccan al-Āla preserves eleven canonical nubat (suites), Algerian gharnati and san'a preserve overlapping suite-cycles, Tunisian ma'luf preserves thirteen nubat, and Libyan ma'luf preserves a smaller set in the same family. Each nuba is a multi-movement suite organized around a single maqam (modal-cycle), comprising five canonical movements: mizan al-busayt (slow-opening rhythmic-movement), mizan al-qaim wa-nisf (mid-tempo movement), mizan al-btayhi (lighter-tempo middle movement), mizan al-darj (faster movement), and mizan al-quddam (concluding fast-tempo movement). Performance configuration: male choir of cantor-and-chorus (the singers carry the lyric verse, drawn from classical Arabic and Andalusi-period muwashshah strophic poetry and zajal vernacular-Arabic verse) accompanied by the canonical Andalusi ensemble — oud (the canonical Arabic-Andalusi lute), rebab (the two-string spike-fiddle), qanun (the trapezoidal box-zither), nay (the end-blown reed flute), and darbuka or tar percussion. Modal vocabulary draws on the Andalusi-specific tab' modal system (twenty-four named modes in the Moroccan recension), with characteristic microtonal intonation distinct from Mashriq Arabic maqam. Carl Davila's The Andalusian Music of Morocco: al-Āla (Reichert Verlag 2013) and the Maison des Cultures du Monde Inédit W260027 catalog constitute the principal Western-distributed scholarship and recordings. Distinguished from Mashriq Arabic maqam (Iraqi, Egyptian, Levantine) by Andalusi-specific suite-of-five-mizans (vs Mashriq tahrir-miyana-taslim) architecture and Andalusi-specific tab' modal vocabulary; distinguished from neighboring Saharan and West-African Sufi traditions by Andalusi nuba's elite-urban-court-and-chamber (vs popular-religious-or-pastoral) functional context.
